variantrule.name: Compound Checks
entries: Occasionally, as GM, you might put forth a task for your players that is more difficult than they might be prepared for, and that task might have multiple ways to accomplish it, such as asking your operative to make an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} to conceal a device on a highly perceptive individual. This task could be reasonable accomplished with a (Dexterity) Sleight of Hand check or a Charisma ({@skill Deception|sw5e-phb}) check. Rather than choosing between the two possible checks, the player could elect to do both. If they do so, they must make two separate ability checks, but the target DC for the checks should be reduced by 5.

For instance, using the above example, you might set the DC for the initial check to be 25, allowing the character to perform a Dexterity ({@skill Sleight Of Hand|sw5e-phb}) check or Charisma (Deception) check. The player might instead decide to attempt both checks. If they do so, they must instead succeed on a DC 20 Dexterity (Sleight Of Hand) check and a DC 20 Charisma (Deception) check. If they succeed on both checks, they accomplish their task. If the fail on either check, they fail the task regardless of the outcome of the other check.

entries.name: Minimum DC
entries: For even more difficult tasks with multiple possible solutions, characters can attempt even more {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks}. For each ability check beyond the first, the DC should decrease by 5, cumulatively, to a minimum DC of 20. For instance, a DC 30 check could instead be accomplished by two separate DC 25 ability checks or even three DC 20 ability checks, provided there are sufficient different ability checks that could apply.

entries.name: Degrees of Failure
entries: You might also consider implementing degrees of failure if a character attempts to perform compound checks and fails one or more of them. For instance, if a character attempts a compound check with two separate {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks} and fails on one or both, you might determine the outcome for failing both to be significantly worse than only failing one.

variantrule.name: Strenuous Combat
entries: Combat is a stressful activity, both physically and mentally. If you want to add an additional layer to combat to help encourage your players to handle things in a more civilized manner, consider implementing this variant rule.

entries.name: Concluding Combat
entries: At the end of a combat encounter, you might consider having each surviving participant make a Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} to avoid {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion}. The DC for the saving throw is equal to 10 + the number of complete rounds that occurred during the encounter. On a failure, a creature suffers 1 level of exhaustion.

entries.name: More Restful Rest
entries: {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb} is a painful penalty to add to characters, especially if they end up encountering multiple levels of exhaustion over the course of a gaming day. When your players' characters complete a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} with exhaustion from this variant, consider allowing them to spend a Hit Die at the end of that rest to remove one level of exhaustion.

If a character encounters multiple levels of exhaustion due to this variant, they can spend more Hit Dice to remove the additional levels, either during the same rest or separate ones. Each time they do so, however, the effect is cumulative for each additional level. Removing a second level of exhaustion would take two Hit Dice, while a third would take three, and so on. For instance, if a character completes a short rest with two levels of exhaustion from this variant, they could spend one Hit Die to remove one level of exhaustion, or three Hit Dice to remove both. Once a creature has completed a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, the number of Hit Dice to be spent to remove this exhaustion is reduced back to one.

variantrule.name: Ammunition Sizes
entries: For the sake of simplicity, ammunition is shared amongst weapons that deal the same damage type. For instance, {@filter all blasters|items|firearm=true} that deal kinetic damage utilize slug cartridges, while firearm=true that deal energy, ion, or other elemental damage types utilize {@item Power cell|sw5e-phb|power cells}. If you dislike that an {@item Assault cannon|sw5e-phb|assault cannon} and a {@item Blaster pistol|sw5e-phb} utilize the same ammunition, consider the following variant rule.

Slug cartridges and {@item Power cell|sw5e-phb|power cells} are each broken down into five size categories, from Tiny to Huge. These new sized ammunitions only fit in weapons that utilize certain damage values, as shown in the below table.
For those weapons with alternative damage types, you'll want to treat their damage as one step higher. Ion damage should be two steps higher or twice the weapon's damage, whichever is lower.

For instance, a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} which deals 1d8 energy damage would use Medium {@item Power cell|sw5e-phb|power cells}, while a firearm=true that deals 1d4 kinetic damage would use Tiny slug cartridges. A firearm=true that deals 1d4 fire damage, however, would use Small power cells (since we treat that damage as one step higher), as would a firearm=true that deals 1d3 ion damage (since we treat that damage as two steps higher).
Additionally, the value and weight of these sized munitions would scale, as shown in the table below.

entries.name: Powered by Power Cells
entries: Items that are powered by {@item Power cell|sw5e-phb|power cells}, such as jetpacks or glowrods, would utilize Medium power cells.

variantrule.name: Alternate Casting
entries: Inspired by the Dimension 20 actual play campaign A Starstruck Odyssey, where one of the main characters is using sentinel bones but with {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} instead of {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}, I've created the following variant rule.

entries.name: Saving Throws
entries: For the five classes with native casting (consular, engineer, guardian, scout, sentinel) you'll want to make the following adjustments to their {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}.

items: {@b Consular:} Replace Charisma with Intelligence.
{@b Engineer:} Replace Intelligence with Charisma.
{@b Guardian:} Replace Charisma with Intelligence.
{@b Scout:} No changes.
{@b Sentinel:} Replace Charisma with Intelligence.

entries.name: Force- and Tech-casting
entries: You'll want to replace the {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} feature with {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}, and vice versa, as appropriate. Specifically, {@b Force Powers Known}, {@b Force Points}, and {@b Forcecasting Ability} will want to be replaced with {@b Tech Powers Known}, {@b Tech Points}, and {@b Techcasting Ability}, and vice versa, as described below:
Note that Max Power Level is not mentioned because it is not affected by these changes.

items: {@b Consular:} Replace consular {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} with engineer {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}.
{@b Engineer:} Replace engineer {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} with consular {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}.
{@b Guardian:} Replace guardian {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} with scout {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}.

{@b Scout:} Replace scout {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} with guardian {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}. Mechanist scout should instead replace Improved {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} with sentinel {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}.

{@b Sentinel:} Replace sentinel {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} with the Improved {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} present in the Mechanist Technique scout archetype, with the following updates: sentinels will have 5 and 6 {@book Tech Powers Known|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers}, and 2 and 3 tech points, at 1st and 2nd levels, respectively.

{@b Splashcasters:} Replace {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} with {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}, and vice versa, of the other splashcasting archetype for that class. For instance, Shield Specialist fighter would replace its {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} feature with {@book Adept Specialist|sw5e-ec|1|Adept Specialist} fighter's {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}.

entries: For the crosscaster archetypes, such as Way of {@skill Technology|sw5e-phb} consular, you can simply flip the powers accordingly.

entries.name: Class Features
entries: Different classes or archetypes with casting as a core component are typically built around that casting's primary ability score. You'll want to update or replace them, as appropriate to the class or archetype, including capstones.

entries.name: Short or Long Rest Recovery
entries: You can also consider swapping the point recovery rest requirements, creating {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} force points or {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} tech points. To do so, you'll want to halve the base number of force points (not accounting for ability modifier) to account for short rest recovery, or double the base number of tech points (again not accounting for ability modifier) to account for long rest recovery. For instance, a consular with long rest {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} gets four tech points for each consular level (before modifier). If you wanted to do a short rest 10 consular instead, you'd only receive two tech points per consular level. The opposite would be true for an engineer; while they would get two tech points per engineer level as with short rest recovery {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}, they would instead get four tech points per engineer level for long rest casting (again, ignoring additional tech points from their ability modifier).
Note that if you are only swapping the rest mechanics, this has no impact on powers known or casting ability, as discussed earlier in this variant rule.

entries.name: Sundry Sidney
entries: For those of you watching A Starstruck Odyssey, Sundry Sidney is a sentinel using {@book techcasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} instead of {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting}. While they swapped the powers known, type of points, and casting ability, they maintained the {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} recovery of points. Consequently, she kept the three points per level a sentinel would normally receive, instead of halving the number received as with Improved 10 present in the Mechanist Scout archetype.

variantrule.name: Invocation Versatility
entries: With the semi-recent release that added a second level of customization classes that lack them—collectively referred to as invocations, due to their inspiration from the warlock feature of that name—every class now has two levels of customization available to them: their class's invocation feature, and their archetype. Most (all?) of the class's invocation features are hard-locked; that is, once you choose it, you've got it for life. Benevolent GMs might allow players to replace a choice if they found it underwhelming, but others might not. With this variant rule, however, it is encouraged for GMs to allow their player's to rechoose invocations {@i on a case-by-case basis.}

entries.name: What are Invocations?
entries: Beyond their choice of archetype, each class has a second level of customization collectively referred to as invocations. These invocations are as follows:

items: Berserkers have Berserker Instincts.
Consulars have Force-Empowered Casting.
Engineers have Modification Slots, which vary based on their class.
Fighters have their Combat Superiority Maneuvers.
Guardians have their Guardian Auras.
Monks have their Monastic Vows.
Operatives have their Operative Exploits.
Scholars have their Academic Superiority Maneuvers {@i and} Discoveries.
Scouts have their Scout Routines.
Sentinels have their Sentinel Ideals.

entries: Of the ten classes, only engineers (mostly), fighters, and scholars can re-choose their invocations, and even then only sparingly. Using this rule, you can instead let all ten classes re-choose their invocations, at appropriate intervals.

entries.name: When Can They Re-choose?
entries: The easiest route would be to allow characters to re-choose one of their invocation options when they complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, or even when they level up. Alternatively, you might enforce a narrative moment for them to re-choose. For instance, a guardian might not be able to relearn their Guardian Aura without spending some time with their master, while a monk might have to spend time in a monastery to re-choose a Monastic Vow, and a scout might have to spend time alone practicing to re-choose a Scout Routine. Ultimately, the method in which allow your players to re-choose their invocations is up to you and your playgroup. You might even let them re-choose on the fly.

entries.name: Re-choosing Archetypes or Classes?
entries: Re-choosing archetypes or classes is not intended as a part of this variant rule. However, you could easily allow players to do so, though I'd recommend the narrative approach over the simple level up or {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

variantrule.name: Elevation
entries: One aspect of 5e that has been more-or-less untouched is the concept of using elevation to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} beyond just creatures not being able to reach you. This variant rule offers mechanical boons to encourage utilizing elevation as a tactical device. Elevation grants a bonus called dominance, which comes in three levels.

A creature has {@b dominance} over another creature if it is at least 10 feet above that creature vertically, and at least 10 feet away from that creature horizontally. While a creature has dominance over another, it has a +2 bonus to ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} against the dominated creature, and the dominated creature suffers a -2 penalty to Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against effects the creature dominating it controls. Additionally, a creature with dominance has a +2 bonus to AC and Dexterity saving throws against a creature it is dominating.

A creature has {@b superdominance} over another creature if it is at least 20 feet above that creature vertically, and at least 20 feet away from that creature horizontally. While a creature has superdominance over another, it has a +3 bonus to ranged attack rolls against the superdominated creature, and the superdominated creature suffers a -3 penalty to Dexterity saving throws against effects the creature dominating it controls. Additionally, a creature with superdominance has a +3 bonus to AC and Dexterity saving throws against a creature it is dominating.

A creature has {@b hyperdominance} over another creature if it is at least 30 feet above that creature vertically, and at least 30 feet away from that creature horizontally. While a creature has hyperdominance over another, it has a +5 bonus to ranged attack rolls against the hyperdominated creature, and the hyperdominated creature suffers a -5 penalty to Dexterity saving throws against effects the creature dominating it controls. Additionally, a creature with hyperdominance has a +5 bonus to AC and Dexterity saving throws against a creature it is dominating.

A creature can only benefit from one level of dominance at a time for each creature it would be dominating, but it can have different levels of dominance for different creatures. For instance, if a creature is 30 feet above another creature both vertically and horizontally, it is hyperdominating that creature. If it is 20 feet above another creature vertically and 15 feet horizontally, it is only dominating the third creature instead of superdominating, since both values exceed 10 feet, but not 20.

entries.name: Advantage and Disadvantage
entries: If a creature has {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, it can choose to forgo that advantage when making an attack to increase its domination level by one against its target until the end of its turn. For instance, if a creature has advantage and is 20 feet above another creature both vertically and horizontally, it is superdominating that creature. The creature can choose to forgo its advantage to instead hyperdominate the creature until the end of its turn.
If a creature is suffering from {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, it can't dominate another creature regardless of how far away from that creature it is, horizontally or vertically.

entries.name: Cover
entries: If a creature would be dominating another creature, and it also has {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover} from that creature, the bonus to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} don't stack. Instead, the dominating creature gains the higher of the two bonuses. For instance, if a creature is dominating another creature, and it also has half cover from that creature, it only gains the +3 bonus to AC and Dexterity saving throws against that creature. However, if the dominated creature has a feature that allows it to ignore the benefit of cover, such as {@optfeature Sharpshooter Mastery|sw5e-phb}, the dominating creature would still gain the +2 benefit from dominating the other creature.

Conversely, if a creature is both dominated by another creature, and it has cover from that creature, you don't add the bonus and penalty together. Instead, you reduce a creatures dominance by one for each level of cover it has. For instance, if a creature is superdominated by a creature, but it also has one-quarter cover from that creature, it is instead just dominated. If the creature that is dominating it has a feature that allows it to ignore the benefit of cover, such as a Sharpshooter Mastery, however, the creature is still superdominated since the creature dominating it isn't affected by the cover.

variantrule.name: Gestalt and Dichotomous Characters
entries: Best suited for smaller parties, gestalt and dichotomous Characters are two separate variant rules that have some conceptual overlap. Gestalt focuses on a character having two classes simultaneously, while, dichotomous focuses on having one class, with two archetypes. If either—or Ashla forbid, both—of these concepts sound intriguing to you, consider the following variant rules.

entries.name: Gestalt Characters
entries: As indicated above, gestalt characters level in two classes simultaneously. They gain all of the proficiencies and features of each class, with following adjustments.

entries.name: Experience Gain
entries: Because a character is leveling in two classes simultaneously, the amount of experience that character should require to gain a level should double. For instance, going from 2nd level to 3rd requires 600 experience points. For a gestalt character, it instead requires 1,200.

entries.name: Hit Points and Hit Dice
entries: If a character chooses two classes with different sized Hit Dice, they should take the average of the two Hit Die sizes (rounded down), and they don't add the Hit Dice together. For instance, if a gestalt character chooses to level in consular, who has a {@dice d6} Hit Die, and guardian, who has a {@dice d10} Hit Die, that character would have a {@dice d8} Hit Die. If the player chooses consular and sentinel, who has a d8 Hit Die, however, their Hit Die would be a d6, since that would be the average of the two Hit Die sizes rounded down.

entries.name: Starting Proficiencies and Equipment
entries: For starting proficiencies and equipment, what you receive varies:
{@b {@i Saving Throws.}} You choose the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} pair offered by either class. You cannot mix-and-match, and you do not get both.
{@b {@i Skills.}} You choose the skills offered by one of your classes. You cannot mix-and-match, and you do not get both.
{@b {@i Weapons, Armor, and Tools.}} You gain the weapons, armor, and tool proficiencies for both classes.
{@b {@i Starting Equipment.}} You gain the starting equipment—or starting wealth—for either class. You cannot mix-and-match, and you do not get both.

entries.name: Ability Score Increases
entries: When a gestalt character reaches 4th, 8th, 12th, 16th, and 19th level, they gain the Ability Score Improvement feature in both classes. At each of these levels, that character should only gain this feature once, instead of twice. Alternatively, you can give them the full +2 Ability Score Improvement from one class, and a feat from the other, as with the ASI and a Feat variant rule.

entries.name: Force- and Tech-Casting
entries: If a character chooses two classes that both have force- or tech-casting, they use the following adjustments:

items: They determine their Max Power Level as if they were multiclassing. If the potential Max Power Level of the two classes combined would exceed 9, however, they instead use the fullcasting Max Power Level progression present on the Multiclass Max Power Level table.
They add the force or tech points from both classes together.
They learn their powers separately by class, as with multiclassing, and those powers are restricted by that class's native Max Power Level regardless of their gestalt Max Power Level.

entries: If a character chooses two classes with opposing casting, they ignore these rules. For instance, if a gestalt character levels as consular and scout, force- and tech-casting are treated separately as determined by their class.

entries.name: Overlapping Features
entries: If two classes receive features that overlap, and aren't otherwise mentioned, it's up to the GM to determine how those features interact.

entries.name: Multiclassing
entries: Gestalt Characters are not suitable for multiclassing.

entries.name: Dichotomous Characters
entries: Instead of your character leveling in two classes simultaneously, you can have your character level in one class, but with two archetypes from that class.

When a character reaches third level, they gain an archetype of their choice for their chosen class. Using this variant, they instead can choose two. At each level within that class that they would gain archetype features, they gain the features for both archetypes. If archetypes offer features that conflict, it's up to the GM to determine how those features interact.
Alternatively, you can have a dichotomous character choose the features of only one archetype at a given level, rather than both, allowing the player to mix and match archetype features.

entries.name: Multiclassing
entries: If a dichotomous character multiclasses, and reaches third level in two or more classes, it's up to the GM to determine whether they gain multiple archetypes in each class, or only in one.

entries.name: Gestalt and Dichotomous
entries: Gestalt and dichotomous characters, since they impact only certain parts of the character generation experience, work seamlessly together. Simply follow the rules associated with gestalt characters, including the restriction on multiclassing, and allow them to choose two archetypes in each class at 3rd level.

variantrule.name: Called Shots
entries: Often times, in combat, characters might want to target a specific body part or feature of their target when making an attack. This is commonly referred to as a "called shot." If this is a mechanic you want to implement in your game, consider using the following variant rule.

entries.name: Calling A Shot
entries: In order to make a called shot, you must first be making an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}. If you want to turn that attack into a called shot, you can choose to do so by forgoing that advantage. If you do so, and the attack hits, the hit becomes a called shot.

When you hit with a called shot, you can choose to deal normal weapon damage and then roll a d100 to determine the effect of the shot randomly using the Called Shot Effects table below. Alternatively, you can choose to roll your damage dice twice and take the lesser total. If you do so, you can choose the effect you want to cause on the Called Shot Effects table below, instead of determining it randomly.

rows: {@b {@i Leg Shot.}} The creature gains 1 {@condition Slowed|sw5e-phb|slowed} level until the end of its next turn.
{@b {@i Arm Shot.}} The creature can not use an arm until the end of its next turn. If the creature has multiple arms, determine which arm is affected randomly.

{@b {@i Scatter Shot.}} If the creature attempts to cast a power before the end of its next turn, it must first make a {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} check (DC = 10 + the power's level). On a failure, any resources are spent and the power immediately fails.
{@b {@i Head Shot.}} The creature is {@condition Blinded|sw5e-phb|blinded} until the start of its next turn.
entries.caption: Called Shot Effects

variantrule.name: Bonus Proficiencies
entries: Unlike traditional 5e, Star Wars 5e places a significantly greater emphasis on the use of tools. Additionally, Star Wars 5e has substantially more languages than traditional 5e, since it spans an entire galaxy, with hundreds if not thousands of species, each speaking their own language. Using this variant rule, you can add additional proficiencies in tools and languages to your players beyond those offered by their species, class, or background.

entries.name: Proficiency Points
entries: Each character gains a number of proficiency points equal to their {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. These proficiency points can be spent to learn languages or tool proficiencies at a ratio of 1 point per language or tool.

entries.name: Tool Expertise
entries: If a character wants to instead use their points to gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a tool, the GM might allow them to spend 2 proficiency points to gain expertise in a tool in which they are already proficient.

entries.name: When Are They Chosen?
entries: Each character can choose to spend their proficiency points at any time to gain proficiency in a language or tool. If they would do so in a moment when that language or proficiency would become relevant to the story, they must first justify how they already know that language or tool proficiency. For instance, if the party encounters a particular species from which they need to glean information, and they have no way to communicate with that species, one of your players might spend a proficiency point to learn the language that species speaks. In order to do so, however, they must first explain how they would know that language. Perhaps they grew up with a wandering member of that species who taught it to them? Or maybe they took this specific language as an elective during their education?

entries.name: Alternative Proficiencies
entries: Alternatively, you might allow your players to spend their proficiency points to gain proficiency in weapons or armor. A character could spend 1 proficiency point to gain proficiency in a singular weapon, or 2 proficiency points to gain proficiency in a weapon category ({@filter all blasters|items|firearm=true}, {@filter lightweapons|items|type=martial weapon|category=lightweapon}, or {@filter vibroweapons|items|type=martial weapon}). A character could also spend 2 proficiency points to gain proficiency in a type of armor. However, they would first need to have proficiency in the lesser armors. For instance, to gain proficiency in {@filter heavy armor|items|type=heavy armor}, you must first have proficiency in {@filter medium armor|items|type=medium armor}. To gain proficiency in type=medium armor, you must first have proficiency in {@filter light armor|items|type=light armor}.

entries.name: Skill Expertise
entries: If a character wants to instead use their points to gain {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a skill, the GM might allow them to spend 4 proficiency points to gain expertise in a skill in which they are already proficient.

variantrule.name: Alternative At-Wills and Extra Attack
entries: One of my many gripes with 5e is that its cantrips scale with character level. I find that this doesn't make sense both mechanically and logically; if I multiclass 2 levels of fighter and 3 levels of warlock, I don't magically get Extra Attack, but for some reason I can create two beams when I cast {@i eldritch blast}. If you want to try alternative at-will power scaling, consider this variant rule.

entries.name: Caster Level
entries: Instead of having at-will powers that improve at 5th, 11th, and 17th {@i character} level, instead have them scale at 5th, 11th, and 17th {@i caster} level. Caster level is, effectively, what you're calculating when you are determining your Max Power Level while multiclassing.

To determine your caster level, you divide your class's potential Max Power Level by 9, and then multiply the result by your number of levels in that class. That number is your caster level. For the full-caster classes—consular and engineer—this will be the same as your level in that class. For other casting classes and archetypes, your caster level will be lower than your level in that class.

When multiclassing, you determine your caster level by dividing each class's potential Max Power Level by 9, multiplying the result by the number of levels in that class, adding the results for each class together, and rounding down the final result. For instance, if you have four levels in Marauder Approach berserker (1.77) and three levels in guardian (1.67), your caster level is 3.

entries.name: Results
entries: Ultimately, the results of this variant rule mean that a 20th-level fighter who took the {@feat Force-Sensitive|sw5e-phb} feat and the {@i shock} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} is no longer as potent with shock as a 20th-level consular. Both mechanically and flavorfully, this aligns to me. Additionally, it means the consular who focuses on the Force is also better with their at-will powers than an equal level guardian or sentinel, which again makes more sense mechanically and flavorfully.

entries.name: Favored At-Wills
entries: Some archetypes, such as most sentinel archetypes or Soresu guardian, are built around a specific at-will. Your GM might consider letting characters of that archetype use native scaling. However, if adopting this variant rule, they should only scale with class level in this way, rather than character level.

entries.name: Multiclassing Extra Attack
entries: If using this variant rule, you might consider allowing characters who multiclass in classes with the Extra Attack feature to add their class levels together to gain that feature. Their combined level in those classes must satisfy the level requirement in both classes to receive this benefit, however.

For instance, a character with 2 levels in fighter and 3 levels in berserker would be eligible for Extra Attack, since their combined levels would meet the 5th-level requirement for Extra Attack in both classes.

On the other hand, a character with 2 levels in fighter and 3 levels in armormech engineer, would not be eligible for Extra Attack, since their combined levels levels don't meet the 6th-level requirement for Extra Attack in armormech engineer. If that character gains an additional level in either class, or a level in another class with the Extra Attack feature, however, they would now meet the requirements for Extra Attack in all three classes, and thus would gain the feature.

If a class or archetype has a restriction to their Extra Attack feature, such as armormech engineer requiring that you are wearing your modified armor or wielding your modified shield to gain the benefit, the character must meet that requirement to gain the benefits of Extra Attack while multiclassing.

entries.name: Greater Extra Attack
entries: No characters should receive the Greater Extra Attack feature through this multiclassing variant, since that feature is exclusive to fighter.

variantrule.name: Longer Rests
entries: SW5e offers greater character customization than traditional 5e, and ultimately yields more powerful characters. If you find yourself struggling to challenge your party, consider using the following variant rule to make them stretch their resources.

entries.name: Quick Rest
entries: A quick rest is a period of downtime, at least 1 hour long, during which a character does nothing more strenuous than eating, drinking, reading, and tending to wounds.

A character can spend one or more Hit Dice at the end of a quick rest, up to the character's maximum number of Hit Dice, which is equal to the character's level. Whenever a character spends a Hit Die to regain {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, the player rolls the die and adds the character's Constitution modifier to it. The character regains hit points equal to the total. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll.

entries.name: Short Rest
entries: A {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} is a period of extended downtime, at least 8 hours long, during which a character sleeps for at least 6 hours and performs light activity, such as reading, talking, eating, or standing watch, for no more than 2 hours. If the rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity—fighting, casting powers, at least 4 hours of walking, or similar adventuring activity—the characters must restart the rest to benefit from it.

At the end of a short rest, a character regains missing {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} up to half their hit point maximum (rounded up). A character can then spend one or more Hit Dice, up to the character's maximum number of Hit Dice, which is equal to the character's level. Whenever a character spends a Hit Die to regain hit points, the player rolls the die and adds the character's Constitution modifier to it. The character regains hit points equal to the total. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll.
A character can't benefit from more than one short rest in a 24-hour period, and a character must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.

entries.name: Long Rest
entries: A {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} is a period of extended downtime, at least 2 days long, during which a character sleeps for at least 6 hours each day, and performs light activity, such as reading, talking, eating, or standing watch during the remainder of the long rest. If the rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity—fighting, casting powers, at least 4 hours of walking, or similar adventuring activity—the characters must restart the rest to benefit from it.

At the end of a long rest, a character regains all lost {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. The character also regains spent Hit Dice, up to a number of dice equal to half of the character's total number of them (minimum of one).
A character can't benefit from more than one long rest in a 7-day period, and a character must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.

entries.name: Power Durations and Other Effects
entries: Certain powers, such as {@i battle precognition} or {@i force barrier}, are powers that are intended to be cast once or twice per adventuring day. Since long rests are now once per week instead of once per day, consider increasing the duration of these powers to 24 hours, or even up to three days, as you deem appropriate.

variantrule.name: Wounds
entries: When a character is reduced to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, begins making {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throws}, and has hit points restored, they can return to the battle no worse for the wear. Using this variant rule, you can add an additional layer to make falling to 0 hit points more threatening.

entries.name: Gaining Wounds
entries: When a character is reduced to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, that character must make a DC 10 Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. On a success, nothing happens, but the DC of this saving throw for that character increases by 5, cumulatively, until they complete a short or {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} or fail the saving throw, at which point the DC resets to 10. On a failed save, the character suffers 1 wounded level. On a success or a failure, a creature immediately gains one {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw} failure for each wounded level it has.

For instance, if a character with no wounded levels is reduced to 0 hit points and fails their Constitution saving throw, they gain 1 wounded level, and they then gain 1 death saving throw failure for their 1 wounded level. Alternatively, if a character with 2 wounded levels is reduced to 0 hit points and succeeds on their Constitution saving throw, they don't gain a wounded level, but they then gain 2 death saving throw failures for their 2 wounded levels. If they take damage, or fail the death saving throw they make at the start of their next turn, they immediately die.

entries.name: Clearing Wounds
entries: A character loses all wounded levels when they are restored to their hit point maximum, whether through consumables, powers, resting, or other means.

variantrule.name: Critical Saving Throws
entries: Unlike {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls}, which have critical hits and critical misses, {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} don't have critical successes or failures. Using this variant rule, you can allow critical successes and failures on saving throws.

entries.name: Critical Success
entries: When a creature rolls a 20 on their {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} against an effect, they automatically succeed on the saving throw, even if the result of their save would not meet or exceed the save DC. Additionally, if they would suffer any effects on a successful save, such as half damage, they treat the effect's damage as if it had rolled the minimum.

entries.name: Critical Failure
entries: When a creature rolls a 1 on their {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} against an effect, they automatically fail the saving throw, even if the result of their save would meet or exceed the save DC. Additionally, if the effect would deal damage, they treat the effect's damage as if it had rolled the maximum.

entries.name: Features That Grant Critical Saves
entries: Certain features, such as the Explosives fighting style or the Heavy Weapon Specialization feat, grant the ability for certain {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} to deal critical damage. If you are using this variant rule, instead have them expand the {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} range by 1. For instance, while using this variant rule, a character with the Explosives fighting style would have a critical hit range of 2 on their grenades. Consequently, creatures that roll a 1 or a 2 on the saving throw against their grenades would critically fail their saves.
Additionally, you can consider allowing weapons with the keen property to increase the critical hit range of their burst or rapid properties.

entries.name: Saving Throw Checks
entries: If you use the Saving Throw Checks variant, you would instead allow effects to critically succeed if they would critically hit, and critically fail if they would critically miss, as appropriate.

variantrule.name: Careful Checks
entries: When you spend at least 10 minutes performing an activity that requires an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, that check has consequences for failure, and you don't have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the check, you can choose to make that check carefully, colloquially called "taking 10". If you do so, you treat the check as if you had rolled a 10 on the {@dice d20}. For instance, if you are crafting an item, during resolution you make an Intelligence check with the appropriate tools to determine your d100 Roll Modifier. Instead of rolling the d20, you can make a careful check and take 10, treating the check as if you'd rolled a 10, adding your Intelligence modifier and {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, if you are proficient with the tools.
If you would have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on the check, you can instead take 15.

variantrule.name: Replacing Powers
entries: Often a player might feel restricted because they made a bad power choice, and they don't want to wait until their next level up to do so. If this is a mechanic that suits your players, consider using the following variant rule.

Each time a character completes a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, they can attempt to take one power they know and replace it with another power, as long as that power is not of a higher level than their Max Power Level. If the character knows both force and {@book tech powers|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers}, those powers can only be replaced with another force or {@book tech power|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers}, respectively.

The character immediately unlearns the power they are trying to replace, and then must make a force- or tech-casting {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} (using Wisdom or Charisma as appropriate, depending on {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} alignment) with proficiency. The DC of the check varies depending on the level of the power the character is attempting to learn, as shown in the Power Level Check DC table below.

On a success, the new power is learned. On a failure, the new power is not learned, the old power is still forgotten, and the character can't try again until their next {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.
When attempting to replace a power, if the character currently has a vacant power known slot, they do not need to first unlearn a power before attempting to fill that slot.

variantrule.name: Exertion
entries: When the outlook of a situation is grim, player's might want to have their character attempt to go above and beyond, fueling their endeavors with their own vitality at the expense of potentially overexerting themselves through use of this variant rule.

entries.name: Exert
entries: Once per round, a player can have their character attempt to exert themselves. When the character makes an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, or {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, the character can roll a Hit Die without expending it, adding the result of the die to the roll. Alternatively, on their turn, the character can roll a Hit Die without expending it, increasing their {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} by 5 x the amount rolled until the end of their turn. If the character has Hit Dice of different sizes, they can choose which Hit Die they use.
The character can wait until after it rolls the {@dice d20} before deciding to exert themselves, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails.

entries.name: Over-Exertion
entries: When a character exerts themselves, they immediately lose {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to the amount rolled, which can't be reduced or negated in any way. If this damage would reduce the character to 0 hit points, they don't immediately fall {@condition Unconscious|sw5e-phb|unconscious}. At the end of the current turn, if the character is still at 0 hit points, they fall unconscious and are stable.

variantrule.name: Simplified Styles and Masteries
entries: In lieu of the fighting style and fighting mastery options available in the PHB, using this variant rule you can instead use the options present here.

entries.name: Fighting Styles
entries: Certain class features or feats offer your choice of Fighting Style. Choose from the following. You can't take a Fighting Style option more than once, even if you later get to choose again.

entries.name: Brawling
entries: You are skilled at using your weight to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}. You gain the following benefits:

items: You are proficient with improvised weapons.
Your unarmed strike damage increases by one step (from 1 to {@dice d4}, {@dice d4} to {@dice d6}, or {@dice d6} to {@dice d8}).

When you attempt to shove or grapple a creature, or make an attack against a creature with an unarmed strike or an improvised weapon wielded in one hand on your turn, you can use your {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to make an additional attack, grapple, or shove against the same creature.

entries.name: Close Quarters Shooting
entries: You are skilled at getting up close and personal with {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons. While you are wielding a firearm=true weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When making a ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack} while you are within 5 feet of a hostile creature, you do not have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}.
Your ranged weapon attacks ignore {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|half cover} against targets within 15 feet of you.
You gain a +1 bonus to {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} you make with {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons.

entries.name: Defense
entries: You are skilled at the art of defending yourself. While you are wearing armor with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to AC.
You have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks} and {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} to avoid being moved.

entries.name: Dueling
entries: You are skilled in the art of fighting with a single melee weapon. While you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain a +2 bonus to damage rolls.

entries.name: Equilibrium
entries: You are skilled at fighting while minimally armored. While you are wearing no armor and not wielding a medium or heavy shield, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to AC.
You gain a +1 bonus to {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} you make with {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|sw5e-phb|unarmed strikes} and weapon attacks.

entries.name: Great Weapon Fighting
entries: You are skilled at putting the weight of a weapon to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}. While you are wielding a melee weapon in two hands with which you are proficient, when you roll a 1 or 2 on a damage die for an attack, you can reroll the die and must use the new roll, even if the new roll is a 1 or a 2.

entries.name: Sentinel
entries: You are skilled at techniques that take {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} of every drop in any enemy's guard. While you are wielding a melee weapon with which you are proficient, you can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to enter a defensive stance that lasts until the start of your next turn. While in your defensive stance, you can make a number of {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks} equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} without using your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, and you can use your Reaction to make a melee attack against a creature that moves more than 5 feet while within your reach.

entries.name: Sharpshooting
entries: You are skilled with {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons and can make shots that others find difficult. While you are wielding a firearm=true weapon with which you are proficient, gain a +2 bonus to ranged weapon attacks.

entries.name: Shielding
entries: You are skilled at using your shield to defend your allies as well as yourself. While you are wielding a shield with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When a creature you can see attacks a target other than you that is within 5 feet of you, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}.
If you are wielding a heavy shield, you are no longer required to wield a weapon with the light property in the other hand.

entries.name: Throwing
entries: You are skilled with the techniques of throwing weapons. While you are wielding a weapon with the thrown property with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to ranged attack and damage rolls.
Whenever you make a ranged attack with a thrown weapon, you can immediately draw another weapon as part of the attack.

entries.name: Two-Weapon Fighting
entries: You are skilled at fighting with two weapons. While you are wielding separate weapons in each hand, or a weapon with the double property, with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you engage in Two-Weapon Fighting, you can add your ability modifier to the damage of your Two-Weapon Fighting attack.
When you make an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}, you can attack with both of your weapons.

entries.name: Versatile Fighting
entries: You are skilled at using weapons in different ways. While you are wielding a melee weapon with the versatile property with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} while wielding a weapon in one hand.
You gain a +1 bonus to damage rolls while wielding a weapon in two hands.

entries.name: Fighting Masteries
entries: Certain class features or feats offer your choice of Fighting Mastery. Choose from the following. You can't take a Fighting Mastery option more than once, even if you later get to choose again.

entries.name: Brawling Mastery
entries: You've mastered using your weight to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, easily wrangling targets around. You gain the following benefits:

items: Your improvised weapons use a {@dice d6} for damage and gain the versatile (2d4) property.
Your unarmed strike damage increases by one step (from 1 to {@dice d4}, {@dice d4} to {@dice d6}, or {@dice d6} to {@dice d8}).
Your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} isn't halved by carrying a {@condition Grappled|sw5e-phb|grappled} creature who is the same size category as you or smaller.

Once per turn, when you hit a creature with an unarmed strike or an improvised weapon, you can make an additional unarmed strike or improvised {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack} against the same target without the aid of your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} (no action required).

entries.name: Close Quarters Shooting Mastery
entries: You've mastered getting up close and personal with {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons, maintain both rate of fire and accuracy. While you are wielding a firearm=true weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, you can choose to fire rapidly at the expense of accuracy. Your ranged weapon attacks are made without the aid of your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, but you use your {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to make an additional ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack}, also without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.
Your ranged weapon attacks ignore {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|half cover} against targets within 30 feet of you.

Other creatures provoke an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack} from you when they move to within 15 feet of you, and you can use {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons when making {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks}.

entries.name: Defense Mastery
entries: You've mastered the art of defending yourself, treating your armor as a second skin. While you are wearing armor with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: Critical hits made against you are treated as normal hits.
When a creature makes a melee attack against you and misses, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to attempt to shove that creature up to 10 feet directly away from you.

entries.name: Dueling Mastery
entries: Your mastery of fighting with a single melee weapon is unsurpassed; you make one weapon feel like many. While you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, you can decide to attack with haste at the expense of accuracy. Your melee weapon attacks are made without the aid of your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, but you use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to make an additional {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack}, also without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.

When a creature hits you with a melee attack, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to add your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to your AC for that attack, potentially causing the attack to miss you.

entries.name: Great Weapon Mastery
entries: You've mastered putting the weight of a weapon to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, letting its momentum empower your strikes. While you are wielding a melee weapon in two hands with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: On your turn, when you score a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} with a melee weapon or reduce a creature to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} with one, you can make one {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} as a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}.

Before you make a melee attack with a weapon that you are wielding in two-hands with which you are proficient with, you can choose to forgo your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. If the attack hits, you add double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to the attack's damage.

entries.name: Sentinel Mastery
entries: You've mastered techniques to take {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} of every drop in any enemy's guard; in tight spaces you are indomitable. While you are wielding a melee weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you hit a creature with an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}, the creature's {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} becomes 0 for the rest of the turn.
Creatures within 5 feet of you provoke {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks} from you even if they take the {@action Disengage|sw5e-phb} action before leaving your reach.

entries.name: Sharpshooting Mastery
entries: You have mastered {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons and can easily make shots that others find impossible. While you are wielding a firearm=true weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: Attacking at long range doesn't impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on your ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack rolls}.
Your ranged weapon attacks ignore {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|half cover} and three-quarters {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover}.

Before you make an attack with a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon that you are proficient with, you can choose to forgo your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. If the attack hits, you add double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to the attack's damage.

entries.name: Shielding Mastery
entries: You've mastered using a shield to defend your allies as well as yourself, and you understand that shields are not just for protection but also for offense. While you are wielding a shield with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: If you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action on your turn, you can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to try to shove a creature within 5 feet of you with your shield.

If you aren't {@condition Incapacitated|sw5e-phb|incapacitated}, you can add your shield's AC bonus to any Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} you make against a power or other harmful effect.

entries.name: Throwing Mastery
entries: You've mastered the techniques of throwing weapons, readily blending the weapons with your movements. While you are wielding a weapon with the thrown property with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} you make with thrown weapons.
Attacking at long range doesn't impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on your ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack rolls} with thrown weapons.

When you hit a creature with a ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack} with a thrown weapon, you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on your next {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} against that creature before the end of your next turn.
You can use Two-Weapon Fighting even when the melee weapons you are wielding in one hand aren't light, if at least one of them has the thrown property.

entries.name: Two-Weapon Mastery
entries: You've mastered fighting with two weapons, becoming a flurry of motion. While you are wielding separate weapons in each hand, or a weapon with the double property, with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: While wielding separate weapons in each hand, you gain a +1 bonus to AC.
While wielding a double weapon, when you roll a 1 on a weapon damage die, you can reroll the die and must use the new roll, even if the new roll is a 1.
You can engage in Two-Weapon Fighting even when the weapons you are wielding lack the light property.
You can draw or stow two weapons when you would normally be able to draw or stow only one.

When you engage in Two-Weapon Fighting, you can choose to forgo your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. If you do so, you can make an additional Two-Weapon Fighting attack, also without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.

entries.name: Versatile Mastery
entries: You've mastered the art of using weapons in different ways, altering your attack patterns mid-swing. While you are wielding a melee weapon with the versatile property with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you are the target of a {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack}, you can immediately use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to make a {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} against the target without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. On a hit, you impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} made against you.

If you miss an attack while wielding a weapon in two hands, you can immediately make an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} against the same target using one hand. You can only make this attack once per turn. If the two-handed attack was made with {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} or without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, this attack is made the same way.

If you miss an attack while wielding a weapon in one hand, you can immediately attempt to shove that creature up to 5 feet directly away from you. You can only make this attempt once per turn. If the one-handed attack was made with {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} or without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, this {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} is made the same way.

variantrule.name: Tactical Initiative
entries: Rather than each player character and creature acting on their own, two or more allied creatures can instead choose to act tactically and work together using this {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} variant rule.

entries.name: Rolling Tactical Initiative
entries: When combat begins and {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} would be rolled, two or more allied creatures can choose to work as a unit, provided they can see or hear and understand each other. When they do so, they each roll initiative separately, adding any modifiers as appropriate. Once each individual party has rolled their initiative, the group then acts using the lowest result. Once a tactical group is formed, each character's initiative is set to the lowest result, even if the tactical group separates.
For instance, if three players want to use tactical initiative, and they roll a 17, an 11, and a 14, all three players will instead act on initiative 11.

entries.name: Multiple Tactical Groups
entries: The party can use multiple tactical groups rather than all working in concert. For instance, a party of five might split into a tactical group of three and a tactical group of two, each group rolling their tactical {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} separately. A character can only belong to one tactical group at a time.

entries.name: Acting in Concert
entries: When a tactical group's turn comes up in the {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} order, each member of the group acts together. Their turns and actions can come in any order, though each individual tactical group member is still limited to what actions they could normally take. Additionally, actions that could normally be broken up, such as when a fighter takes the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action and has the Extra Attack feature, can be broken up during the turn.

For instance, a 5th-level fighter might take the Attack action and make their first attack. Before they make their second attack, however, the operative ally in their tactical group might then take the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action to grant them {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} before the fighter makes the second attack.

entries.name: Separating a Tactical Group
entries: When a tactical group loses contact with each other, or if the tactical group chooses to break up on their turn (no action required), the tactical group becomes separated. When separated, each member of the former tactical group acts on their own, though they retain the {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} of the tactical group. The order of any active members of the former tactical group acting on the same initiative is determined randomly.

variantrule.name: Alternative Armor
entries: Traditionally, {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb|armor class} is designed entirely for avoidance. While unarmored or lightly armored, that's dodging the attack entirely. In medium or {@filter heavy armor|items|type=heavy armor}, however, that's absorbing the attack on your armor in such a way that it deals no damage. If you want a different approach to armor, try this variant rule.

entries.name: Armor Class (AC)
entries: Base {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb|armor class} (AC), without consideration of any special traits, class features, or armor and shields, is always calculated as 10 + Dexterity modifier, with armor replacing or augmenting that base AC calculation. Using this system, your base armor class is instead calculated as follows:
{@b Base AC} = 8 + your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} + your Dexterity modifier

entries.name: Damage Reduction (DR)
entries: Damage reduction (DR) is a static value that you subtract when you take damage if certain conditions are met. Certain features, such as the Defense fighting mastery or the absorptive armor property, grant DR that only applies when you take damage from weapons. DR is expressed as a number. DR provided by armor only affects damage you take as a result of being hit by an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, in the same way that AC only helps you avoid being hit by an attack roll.
If passive DR would reduce the damage you take to 0, you instead take 1 damage.

entries.name: Armor Class vs. Damage Reduction
entries: Instead of focusing solely on damage avoidance, this variant rule balances {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb|armor class} and damage reduction, to better emphasize how armor is used. Each type of armor affects your AC and DR differently, as shown below.

entries.name: Light Armor
entries: As normal, {@filter light armor|items|type=light armor} does not prohibit the maximum Dexterity bonus you can receive to your AC. However, if the type=light armor had a higher base AC, extra AC instead becomes damage reduction (DR).

For instance, {@item Fiber armor|sw5e-phb|fiber armor} normally increases your AC to 12 + Dexterity modifier. If you have a Dexterity modifier of +3, while wearing fiber armor you would have an AC of 15. With this variant rule, however, fiber armor instead grants you DR of 2 while allowing you to add your Dexterity modifier to your AC. If you have a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2, you would have an AC of 13 (8 + your Proficiency Bonus of +2 and your Dexterity modifier of +3) and DR of 2.

entries.name: Medium Armor
entries: {@filter medium armor|items|type=medium armor} strikes a balance between AC and DR. As normal, it still allows you to add up to +2 to your AC if your Dexterity modifier is +2 or higher.

For instance, {@item Weave armor|sw5e-phb|weave armor} normally increases your AC to 14 + Dexterity modifier (max 2). If you have a Dexterity modifier of +2 or higher, while wearing weave armor you would have an AC of 16. With this variant rule, however, weave armor instead grants you DR of 4 while allowing you to add your Dexterity modifier (max 2) to your AC. If you have a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2, you would have an AC of 12 (8 + your Proficiency Bonus of +2 and your Dexterity modifier of +2) and DR of 4.

entries.name: Heavy Armor
entries: {@filter heavy armor|items|type=heavy armor} focuses entirely on DR. You gain no benefit to AC from your Dexterity modifier, but you also aren't penalized if your Dexterity modifier is negative.

For instance, {@item Assault armor|sw5e-phb|assault armor} normally increases your AC to 17. With this variant rule, however, assault armor instead grants you DR of 7, but it grants no benefit to your AC. If you have a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2, you would have an AC of 10 (8 + your Proficiency Bonus of +2) and DR of 7.

entries.name: Unarmored Defense and Natural Armor
entries: Certain species (such as wookie or colicoid), classes (such as monk or berserker), or archetypes (such as {@book Blademaster Specialist|sw5e-ec|1|Blademaster Specialist} fighter) grant unarmored defense or natural armor. When using this variant, the following rules apply.

{@b {@i Unarmored Defense.}} If your unarmored defense includes Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence, Wisdom, or Charisma, you add that modifier to your AC as normal. If your unarmored defense includes your Constitution modifier, however, you instead treat that modifier as DR. For instance, a monk with a {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} of +2, a Dex modifier of +4, and a Wisdom modifier of +3 would have an AC of 17. A berserker with a Proficiency Bonus of +2, a Dex modifier of +4, and a Constitution modifier of +3, however, would have an AC of 14 and DR of 3.

{@b {@i Natural Armor.}} If your natural armor includes an adjustment to your base AC, that adjustment instead becomes DR. If your natural armor allows you to add your Dexterity modifier to your AC, you still add it as normal. For instance, a wookiee's hide grants them a base AC of 13 + Dexterity modifier. If the wookiee has a Proficiency Bonus of +2 and a Dexterity modifier of +2, instead of having an AC of 15 they would have an AC of 12 and DR of 3. A colicoid, however, who would have an AC of 17, with a Proficiency Bonus of +2, would have an AC of 10 and a DR of 7.

entries.name: Shields
entries: As normal, shields add their bonus to AC.

entries.name: Enhanced Items
entries: If an enhanced armor would add an additional bonus to AC, it instead increases DR. If an enhanced shield would add an additional bonus to AC, it continues to do so. If that bonus only applies to melee or ranged AC, it still only applies to melee or ranged AC or DR, as appropriate.

entries.name: Other AC Calculations
entries: Work with your GM to determine how other AC calculations, such as the {@i battle precognition} power or Way of Endurance consular's Upheld by the Force feature, should translate using these rules.

variantrule.name: Aging
entries: Sometimes, campaigns might take place over years, or even decades. As these campaigns progress, you might want to introduce mechanics to reflect your characters' natural aging. Alternatively, at character creation, you might want to create a character who is already at a later stage in life. Regardless of when your characters have aged, consider using the following variant rule.

Every species ages at a different rate. While many near-human species age at the same rate as humans, reaching adulthood in their late teens, middle age in their 40's, elderly in their late 50's to early 60's, and venerability in their 70's, other species age differently. For instance, lanniks reach adulthood in their 50's and can live up to 900 years, while hutts aren't considered adults until they reach 200 years old and can live to be over a thousand.

Consequently, rather than tying aging to numbers, we instead establish three thresholds: Middle-Age, Elderly, and Venerable. Each time a character reaches one of these thresholds, they gain one or more aging quirks and one or more aging boons, determined by the threshold they've reached. When they do so, the GM can determine choose which quirk and boon they get, or determine it randomly, using the Aging Quirks and Aging Boons tables below:

rows: Your Strength score decreases by 1. Your maximum for this score decreases by 1.
Your Dexterity score decreases by 1. Your maximum for this score decreases by 1.
Your Constitution score decreases by 1. Your maximum for this score decreases by 1.
Your base walking {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} decreases by 5 feet.
entries.caption: Aging Quirks

rows: Your Intelligence score increases by 1. Your maximum for this score increases by 1.
Your Wisdom score increases by 1. Your maximum for this score increases by 1.
Your Charisma score increases by 1. Your maximum for this score increases by 1.
You gain proficiency in a language, skill, tool, or weapon of your choice.
entries.caption: Aging Boons

entries: These effects are cumulative. When a middle-aged character, who has one quirk and one boon, becomes elderly, they gain two more quirks and two more boons, for a total of three of each. Additionally, duplicates are only rerolled at separate thresholds. If, at middle-age, your Strength score decreased by 1, your Strength score could again decrease by 1 at elderly.

entries.name: Middle-Aged
entries: Most species enter middle age about halfway through their expected life. For humans and near-humans, this is typically in their 40's, while lanniks don't reach middle age until about 400 years, and hutts at about 600 years. When a character reaches middle age, the GM should choose one quirk and one boon. Alternatively, they can determine the quirk and boon randomly.

entries.name: Elderly
entries: Like middle age, at which age a species becoming elderly also varies. For humans and near-humans, this is typically in their late 50's to early 60's, while lanniks are considered elderly at about 600, and hutts at about 750 years. When a character becomes elderly, the GM should choose two quirks and two boons. Alternatively, they can determine the quirks and boons randomly, rerolling any duplicates.

entries.name: Venerable
entries: Venerable members of a species are rare and typically revered by the younger members of their species. Humans and near-humans become in their 70's, lanniks at about 750, and hutts over the age of 900. When a character becomes venerable, the GM should choose three quirks and three boons. Alternatively, they can determine the quirks and boons randomly, rerolling any duplicates.

entries.name: Additional Aging Traits
entries: Some species gain additional traits as they age. For instance, hutts have the unique special characteristic in that they never stop growing from birth to death. The GM can add quirks and boons as appropriate for members of those species.

variantrule.name: Force-Bond
entries: When two Force-sensitive individuals spend time together, they can develop a powerful connection through the Force. While bonded in such a fashion, the two individuals gain a series of boons, depending on the strength of their bond. However, if the bond is unwilling, the individuals risk corruption by the dark side of the Force.

entries.name: Developing a Bond
entries: When one creature wants to develop a bond with another, they must spend 1 hour meditating, which can be done during a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest},  while within 30 feet of a target that they can see. At the end of this meditation, the target must make a Charisma {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. The DC of this saving throw is equal to the initiator's universal force save DC, and the target of this feature can choose to fail this save. On a failure, the two creature's develop a Force-bond.

entries.name: Valid Targets
entries: Only sentient creatures who can cast {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st-level or higher can develop a Force-bond, and a creature can only be bonded in such a way to one other creature a time.

entries.name: Strengthening a Bond
entries: In order to strengthen their bond, bond-mates must remain with a certain distance of each other, as shown below in the Bond Distance and DC by Tier table. They must spend one week times the tier they are trying to achieve. For instance, to progress from 1st to 2nd tier takes two weeks, while progressing from 2nd to 3rd takes an additional three weeks. This time does not have to be continuous; bond-mates can spend three days together, two days apart, and then four more days together to achieve 2nd tier.

entries.caption: Bond Distance and DC by Tier

entries.name: Bond Features
entries: At each tier, bond-mates unlock a certain feature. In order to benefit from these features, bond-mates must be within 10 feet of eachother. This distance changes as their bond strengthens, as shown above in the Bond Distance and DC by Tier table.
For instance, at 1st tier, the bond-mates must be within 10 feet of each other to benefit from their bond's features. At 2nd tier, however, they must only be within 30 feet of each other.

entries.name: 1st Tier
entries: Both bond-mates always know precisely where their bond-mate is in relation to them, regardless of whether or not they can see or hear them.

entries.name: 2nd Tier
entries: Both bond-mates can speak with each other as if they were standing within 5 feet, provided they share a language. At 6th tier, this communication becomes telepathic.

entries.name: 3rd Tier
entries: Both bond-mates are constantly under the effects of the {@i sense emotions} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, but they are only able  to read each other's emotions. This does not require    {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} for either bond-mate, and this       feature can not be interrupted while both         bond-mates are conscious.

entries.name: 4th Tier
entries: As an action on each of their turns, bond-mates can pass items to each other. When a bond-mate uses their action in such a way, the other bond-mate must use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to take the item.

entries.name: 5th Tier
entries: Whenever a bond-mate makes an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} or {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} due to the other bond-mate taking the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action, they can reroll one of the dice once.

entries.name: 6th Tier
entries: When a bond-mate casts a {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, they can cast it as if they are standing within 5 feet of their bond-mate. If the power requires a target, and that target is not their bond-mate, they must be aware of the target's presence and location in order to target them with this power.

entries.name: 7th Tier
entries: When a bond-mate casts a power of 1st-level or higher that targets only themself, they can also target their bond-mate.

entries.name: 8th Tier
entries: Whenever a bond-mate is reduced to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, but not killed outright, the other bond-mate can use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to cause them to drop to 1 hit point instead.
Once this feature has been used, neither bond-mate can use it again until they both complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: 9th Tier
entries: On their turn, one bond-mate can use their action to give their bond-mate an additional turn. If they do so, the targeted bond-mate immediately takes an additional turn after the current bond-mate's turn.
Once this feature has been used, neither bond-mate can use it again until they both complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: 10th Tier
entries: Whenever a bond-mate takes damage, the other bond-mate can use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to grant them resistance to the damage. If they do so, both bond-mates take the same amount of damage. Alternatively, when a bond-mate has {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} restored, they can use their Reaction to halve the amount of hit points. If they do so, the other bond-mate regains the same number of hit points. These features can be used a number of times equal to the bond-mate's combined Wisdom or Charisma modifiers (their choice, a minimum of once). All expended uses are regained when both bond-mates complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: Breaking a Bond
entries: Sometimes, creatures might want to end their Force-bond, whether the bond was created unbeknownst to them or they no longer wish to share the bond. To do so, one of the creatures must spend 10 minutes meditating on the bond, and then make a Charisma {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. The DC of this saving throw varies, depending on the tier of the bond, as shown above in the Bond Distance and DC by Tier table. On a success, the bond's tier is reduced by 1. If the bond's tier is 1, it is broken. On a failure, the bond's tier is not reduced, and you can't try again for 24 hours.

variantrule.name: Crueler Criticals
